lesson_title: Series and Parallel: One Road or Two
hook_text: Open a second road and the traffic gets EASIER — that's why your house isn't wired in series.
clip_script: Think of charge as taxis and the battery as the rank. Twelve volts means every taxi leaves loaded with twelve joules. One road only: every taxi passes through both rough patches, so the traffic is identical at every point — and the energy gets shared out, four volts at the four-ohm patch, eight at the eight-ohm patch. Roughness adds: twelve ohms, one amp. Now open a second road. Both routes run between the same two corners, so every taxi drops the full twelve volts on whichever road it takes — not six each, twelve each. What splits is the traffic: three amps down the easy road, one and a half down the rough one, four and a half amps in total. And the combined roughness? Less than either road on its own — two comma six seven ohms. Because opening a road never makes it harder to get through. That's why your house is wired in parallel: every plug gets the full two hundred and thirty volts, and switching off the kettle doesn't switch off the lights.
visual_style: Aerial night-time road map: one glowing loop with traffic crawling evenly, then a junction splitting into two lit routes with counters ticking 3 A and 1,5 A, ending on a house plan with every plug point lighting independently.
pacing: Calm build through the single road, a beat of surprise at the second road opening, confident landing on the house.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and work the 4 Ω and 8 Ω circuit both ways yourself.
